UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                     )          Docket No. ER26-247-000

          MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER OF THE
            SOUTHWEST POWER POOL TRANSMISSION OWNER GROUP

         Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1

American Electric Power Service Corporation, the Evergy Companies, Oklahoma Gas and Electric

Company, and Xcel Energy Services Inc. on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company

(collectively, the SPP TO Group) submit this Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer in

response to comments of Eolian L.P. and Enchanted Rock, LLC on the Southwest Power Pool,

Inc. (SPP) proposal to establish the High Impact Large Load (HILL) and High Impact Large Load

Generation Assessment (HILLGA) processes (together, the HILL Proposal). This Answer first

seeks to correct Eolian’s erroneous suggestion that HILLGA generators will serve load directly.

Load Responsible Entities (LREs), not HILLGA generators, will serve HILLs after selecting

HILLGA generators that meet the LREs’ resource adequacy needs, consistent with the SPP tariff.

Next, the Commission should reject Enchanted Rock’s proposed condition that HILLGA

generators be permitted to exceed the size necessary to meet a HILL’s immediate needs in order

to make future opportunity sales. 2 Enchanted Rock’s proposed condition is a substantial change

to the HILL Proposal that is impermissible under NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC. 3


1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 & .213 (2025).
2
 See Comments of Enchanted Rock, LLC, Docket No. ER26-247 at 6 (Nov. 14, 2025) (Enchanted
Rock Comments) (“The HILLGA Proposal’s current capacity accreditation construct effectively
prevents this excess generation from being studied within the LLRIS framework, and therefore,
any generation above the capacity accreditation cap is excluded from transitioning to ERIS or
NRIS, and from eventually providing firm, reliable power to the grid.” (emphasis added)).
3
    862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017).
 I.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

         The Commission has discretion to accept responses to comments or protests and has

routinely done so for good cause shown where accepting the response would either lead to a more

complete or accurate record, improve the Commission’s understanding of the issues, clarify

disputed or erroneous matters, or help the Commission in its decision-making. 4 There is good

cause for the Commission to accept the SPP TO Group’s answer because it will assist the

Commission in evaluating SPP’s HILL Proposal. 5 Moreover, the SPP TO Group is responding to

comments, not protests, and the text of Rule 213 does not on its face require authorization to

respond to answer comments, as opposed to “a protest, an answer, a motion for oral argument, or

a request for rehearing.” 6

II.      LIMITED ANSWER

         A.      LREs Maintain Responsibility for Retail Service to Load Under the HILL
                 Proposal

         Eolian asks that SPP “clarify that, in providing for a new generator interconnection process

that requires HILLGA Customers to indicate that they will serve a particular HILL, SPP does not

in any way restrict the ability of Interconnection Customers that have obtained or are requesting

[NRIS] through the DISIS process to enter into similar commercial arrangements to serve

particular HILLs.” 7 That clarification is unnecessary because it is founded on a faulty premise.


4
  18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2); see, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 158 FERC ¶ 61,133, at P 12
(2017); KO Transmission Co., 156 FERC ¶ 61,147, at n.5 (2016).
5
  See, e.g., Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 171 FERC ¶ 63,040, at P 20, appeal denied, 172 FERC ¶ 63,008
(2020); Gulf S. Pipeline Co., LP, 145 FERC ¶ 61,236, at P 35 (2013), reh’g denied, 154 FERC
¶ 61,219 (2016); Pioneer Transmission, LLC v. N. Ind. Pub. Serv. Co., 140 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 94
(2012).
6
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a(2).
7
 Comments of Eolian L.P. in Support of SPP’s HILL and HILLGA Processes, Docket No. ER26-
247 at 13 (Nov. 14, 2025) (Eolian Comments) (emphasis added).


                                                  2
 Under SPP’s tariff, it is LREs, not Interconnection Customers, that serve load, including HILLs.

Thus, Eolian’s statement that “[t]he HILLGA process does not condition eligibility on state

support or LRE selection” is also incorrect. 8

           LREs in SPP select the resources they need to meet their resource adequacy needs, subject

to state oversight, as the SPP TO Group explained in SPP’s Expedited Resource Adequacy Study

proceeding. 9 An LRE is “required to offer sufficient resources to cover its expected daily peak

load for the operating day” as part of SPP’s must-offer requirement, 10 and must also bear

responsibility for “self-supplying or bilaterally procuring sufficient capacity to meet its Resource

Adequacy Requirement.” 11 HILLGA generators, like other generators in SPP, are selected by

LREs so that the LRE can fully serve load.

           Denying non-HILLGA Interconnection Customers the same opportunity to contribute to

serving HILLs is not unduly discriminatory or preferential. “[M]ere differential treatment of two

entities does not violate the [FPA].” 12 Rather, “undue discrimination occurs only if the entities are

‘similarly situated,’ such that ‘there is no reason for the difference’” in treatment, 13 and thus,

“according different treatment to different classes of entities … does not amount to undue

9
 See, e.g., Motion for Leave to Answer and Limited Answer of the Southwest Power Pool Load
Responsible Entities, Docket No. ER25-2296 at 6-8 (July 2, 2025); Comments of the Southwest
Power Pool Load Responsible Entities, Docket No. ER25-2296 (June 12, 2025).

     Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 141 FERC ¶ 61,048, at P 35 (2012).
11
     See Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp. v. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 184 FERC ¶ 61,207, at P 3 (2023).
12
  City of Lincoln v. FERC, 89 F.4th 926, 935 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (citing Mo. River Energy Servs. v.
FERC, 918 F.3d 954, 958 (D.C. Cir. 2019)).
13
  Mo. River Energy, 918 F.3d at 958 (quoting State Corp. Comm’n v. FERC, 876 F.3d 332, 335
(D.C. Cir. 2017); Transmission Access Pol’y Study Grp. v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667, 721 (D.C. Cir.
2000)).


                                                   3
 discrimination under the FPA when the classes are not similarly-situated.” 14 SPP has set forth

clear standards that a generator must meet to be selected to serve a HILL. 15 Any generator who

can satisfy those standards can qualify as a HILLGA generator. It is not unduly discriminatory or

preferential to require all generators that want to serve a HILL to satisfy the HILLGA requirements

created for that purpose. 16

         B.     The Commission Should Reject Enchanted Rock’s Proposed Condition to
                Acceptance of the HILL Proposal

         Enchanted Rock requests that the Commission accept the HILLGA process on the

condition that SPP amend Proposed Tariff, Attachment BB, section 3.1.3.2 so that “the projected

capacity accreditation MW value of any generation facilities submitted in a HILLGA Request(s)

may not exceed the associated HILL’s requested load, multiplied by the greater of: 1) 110% plus

the Planning Reserve Margin outlined in the HILLGA Study Agreement; or 2) 150%, rather than

the currently proposed 125% value.” 17 Enchanted Rock asserts that excess generation from a

HILLGA Customer should be eligible to transition to NRIS or ERIS after its LLRIS service


14
 N.J. Bd. of Pub. Utils. v. FERC, 744 F.3d 74, 106 (3d Cir. 2014) (quoting PJM Power Providers
Grp. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 137 FERC ¶ 61,145, at P 109 (2011)).
15
   See Proposed Tariff, Attach. BB § 8.2 (“The HILLGA Customer must submit the following:
(1) an executed HILLGA Study Agreement; (2) a nonrefundable application fee of $20,000; (3) a
study deposit of $250,000 for HILLGA Requests up to 500 MW or a study deposit of $500,000
for HILLGA Requests over 500 MW; (4) demonstration of Site Control; (5) definitive POI;
(6) Nameplate Capacity, Maximum Injection Capability, and Network Resource Deliverability
(MW) pursuant to Appendix 1, Attachment A of Attachment BB; (7) Security deposit equal to
$8,000/MW of the requested Maximum Injection Capability (‘Financial Security One’);
(8) reasonable evidence of satisfaction of one of the listed development milestones; and (9) if
applicable, the charging parameters of the Generating Facility that includes at least one electric
storage resource, and a description of any control technologies that will limit the operation of the
Generating Facility to the operating assumptions submitted by the HILLGA Customer.”).
16
  See Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,062, at P 107 (2025) (accepting SPP’s ERAS proposal
in part because it “applie[d] identical eligibility criteria, and ‘places no limits or priority on
projects based on the resource type or ownership structure’” (emphasis added)).
17
     Enchanted Rock Comments at 6 (bold emphasis in original).


                                                 4
 expires, because, as currently constituted, the HILL Proposal capacity accreditation construct

prevents “any generation above the capacity accreditation cap … from eventually providing firm,

reliable power to the grid.” 18 Essentially, Enchanted Rock argues that a HILLGA generator should

be permitted to exceed the size necessary to meet a HILL’s immediate needs and to make future

opportunity sales.       Enchanted Rock characterizes its proposed condition as a “minimal

modification” that is consistent with NRG. 19 That characterization is incorrect.

           Enchanted Rock abuses NRG, which holds that FPA section 205 “allows FERC to suggest

‘minor’ modifications to a proposal made by a Regional Transmission Organization” but does not

permit the Commission to “make modifications to a proposal that transform the proposal into an

entirely new rate.” 20 That is because, “when FERC ‘imposes an entirely new rate scheme’ in

response to a utility’s proposal, the utility’s customers do not have adequate notice of the proposed

rate changes or an adequate opportunity to comment on the proposed changes.” 21 Utility consent

is required even when the Commission only proposes a minor modification. 22

           The HILL Proposal is clear that the requirement set in Proposed Tariff, Attach. BB, section

3.1.3(2) is meant to “ensure[] that only the generation capacity necessary to serve the HILL is




18
     Id.
19
     862 F.3d 108.
20
     Id. at 110 (citing W. Res., Inc. v. FERC, 9 F.3d 1568, 1579 (D.C. Cir. 1993)).
21
     Id. at 116.
22
   See id. (“A utility’s consent is relevant when FERC proposes ‘minor’ modifications to the
utility’s proposal…. But when FERC proposes its ‘own original notion of a new form of rate,’ the
utility’s consent does not excuse a Section 205 violation.” (quoting W. Res., 9 F.3d at 1579; City
of Winnfield, La. v. FERC, 744 F.2d 871, 875 (D.C. Cir. 1984)); Old Dominion Elec. Coop., 162
FERC ¶ 61,262, at P 35 (2018) (“The Court, however, recognized that in other situations, the
Commission may propose revisions to a section 205 filing that do not amount to an entirely
different rate design or rate scheme, provided that the filing utility consents to the changes.”
(emphasis added)).


                                                    5
 processed through the HILLGA while recognizing the load responsible entities’ requirement to

secure sufficient Resources to cover the Planning Reserve Margin that the load responsible entity

will be required to carry when the HILL receives long-term, firm transmission service.”23

Enchanted Rock’s proposal directly contradicts the SPP HILL Proposal by requesting that

HILLGA generators “eventually provid[e] firm, reliable power to the grid.” 24         Accepting

Enchanted Rock’s proposed condition would not be a “minor modification” to the HILL Proposal,

but a major change that would subvert stakeholder expectations. The entire point of limiting

HILLGA generators to LLRIS interconnection service is to “grant[] limited interconnection rights

solely to support the HILL, which limits both the impacts of the generation on SPP’s Transmission

System and potential Network Upgrade costs.” 25 The Commission should reject Enchanted

Rock’s proposed condition because SPP stakeholders supported, and voted in favor of, the HILL

Proposal in part because it was narrowly-tailored to limit HILLGA generators to serving a

designated HILL; accepting the proposed condition would subvert that fundamental understanding

and would impose “an entirely new rate scheme.” 26

III.     CONCLUSION

         For these reasons, the SPP TO Group respectfully requests that the Commission accept

SPP’s HILL Proposal without modification.
